action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral Hoover sign, collapsing leg weakness, entraining right hand tremor, convergence spasm with miosis and distractibility, with an observed event of typical semiology
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs and observe the event semiology
action_criteria.rationale: Her leg weakness, right hand tremor and events are diagnosed by positive signs incompatible with structural disease and by the semiology of the events (DSM-5 criterion B; Daum 2014); this examination is the diagnostic act.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Video-EEG to record the habitual events
action_criteria.rationale: About eight events with eyes closed, asynchronous jerking and pelvic thrusting continued unchanged on levetiracetam: recording a habitual event without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level, tests for co-occurring epilepsy and decides the taper (LaFrance 2013; AAN 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Levetiracetam without a remaining indication, the serotonergic and bleeding risks of sertraline with cyclobenzaprine and ibuprofen, and the as-needed lorazepam identified
action_criteria.label: Review her medicines before tapering levetiracetam
action_criteria.rationale: Levetiracetam was started for presumed seizures and will be tapered once the events are recorded; she also takes sertraline with cyclobenzaprine and ibuprofen and as-needed lorazepam (AAN 2025; Oto 2005).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild hyponatremia (sodium 132 mEq/L) with normal glucose and calcium
action_criteria.label: Glucose, sodium and calcium
action_criteria.rationale: Nothing in the events suggests a metabolic trigger; a single check is defensible on an SSRI but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast
action_criteria.rationale: The outside head CT was normal and the examination shows positive functional signs with normal reflexes; one non-contrast MRI is defensible but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Profile of the comorbid symptoms that treatment will target; it does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of comorbidity
action_criteria.rationale: A battery with performance-validity measures can quantify her anxiety, low mood and trauma-related symptoms to plan treatment; it costs more than any other step on this pathway and adds nothing to the diagnosis, which rests on the examination.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background reading only; no result in it changes this patient's diagnosis or plan
action_criteria.label: Literature search on FND diagnosis and treatment (background, not a clinical step)
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on the positive diagnosis and treatment of functional neurological disorder; it is not part of this patient's diagnostic pathway and no step of the work-up depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures, or stop it abruptly.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (mixed: functional seizures, functional leg weakness and functional tremor) based on the bilateral Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, tremor entrainment, convergence spasm with miosis and distractibility, and the two habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid anxiety, with a trauma-informed approach.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Taper and stop levetiracetam under neurological supervision, since the events are functional and there is no evidence of epilepsy.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.

avoided_actions.rationale: No palpitations, syncope or cardiac history, and the events have eyes-closed, asynchronous semiology; an ECG answers no question here.
No murmur, cardiac symptom or embolic question; echocardiography answers nothing about her events, tremor or leg weakness.
The events are not syncopal (one to three minutes of asynchronous jerking with eyes closed, rapid recovery); rhythm monitoring answers no question.
A head CT at the outside emergency department four weeks ago was normal; repeating it answers no new question and adds radiation.
No fever, meningism, encephalopathy or inflammatory question; a lumbar puncture is invasive and reinforces the search for an organic cause.
No question in her events, tremor or leg weakness that PET could answer.
Leg weakness with a positive Hoover sign, normal reflexes and no wasting is not neuromuscular; a normal EMG reinforces the search for an organic cause.
Non-dermatomal right leg sensory loss with a midline split is not a question about the somatosensory pathway.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder with psychogenic non-epileptic seizures and functional limb weakness

differential.key_features: Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures. The events continued unchanged on levetiracetam, and eyes closed with resistance to opening, asynchronous movements, pelvic thrusting and rapid recovery also argue against epileptic seizures.

differential.diagnosis: Structural lesion of the brain or spinal cord
differential.key_features: Progressive weakness of both legs raises a cord or parasagittal lesion, but reflexes are normal and symmetric with flexor plantars and no clonus, there is no sensory level or sphincter symptom, and hip extension is full on Hoover testing.

differential.diagnosis: Drug-induced tremor or serotonin toxicity (sertraline with cyclobenzaprine)
differential.key_features: The combination can cause tremor and myoclonus, but her tremor is unilateral, variable, entrains to the other hand and stops when she is absorbed, with no hyperreflexia, clonus, agitation or autonomic signs.

key_clinical_evidence: Positive signs of functional leg weakness: bilateral Hoover sign and collapsing weakness, with a gait that improves during serial subtraction.
Right hand tremor that entrains to left-hand tapping and stops when she is absorbed in an activity; convergence spasm with miosis.
Events with eyes closed and resisting opening, asynchronous limb jerking, side-to-side head movement, pelvic thrusting and rapid recovery; one was observed during the examination.
The 72-hour video-EEG recorded two habitual events without ictal EEG change, with a normal interictal record.
Levetiracetam, started at an outside emergency department for presumed seizures, did not change the events and has no remaining indication.
Anxiety, childhood abuse and a contested separation are supportive context, neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A second-degree relative with epilepsy does not make the patient's events epileptic. The semiology and the video-EEG recording of habitual events without ictal change decide it.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic etiology and pursue prolonged AED trials before confirming PNES with video-EEG

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Generalized anxiety disorder and a prior major depressive episode
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions also flare with stress. A stressor is supportive context, neither required nor sufficient; the positive signs and the recorded events make the diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Onset during a contested separation and custody dispute
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude prematurely that stress 'caused' the symptoms and that the workup can be abbreviated

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A drug started on presumption is not evidence of epilepsy; the events continued unchanged on it, and once habitual events are recorded without ictal change it is tapered.
red_herrings.data_point: Levetiracetam started at an outside emergency department for presumed new-onset seizures
red_herrings.intended_effect: Treat the earlier presumption of epilepsy as established and escalate antiseizure treatment

sequence_constraints.reason: The decision to taper antiseizure drugs rests on the recorded events (AAN 2025; Oto 2005).

findings.result: Hip extension in both legs is stronger during contralateral hip flexion against resistance than on direct testing.
Hip flexion, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion in both legs, right worse than left, give way suddenly after initial full effort.
The right hand tremor takes on the rhythm of left-hand tapping and pauses during ballistic left-hand movements.
Gait improves markedly during serial subtraction.
Intermittent convergent eye deviation with miosis during eye movement testing, resolving spontaneously.

Variable, non-velocity-dependent resistance to passive leg movement; lurching gait with excessive sway but no falls; non-dermatomal right leg sensory loss with midline splitting; vibration loss split across the frontal bone; inconsistent right heel-to-shin performance; not counted as rule-in signs.

About 90 seconds of unresponsiveness with eyes closed and resisting opening, eyelid flutter, asynchronous jerking of all four limbs with variable amplitude, side-to-side head movements and pelvic thrusting, ending gradually; the dropped arm avoided the bedrail.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness and functional tremor: bilateral Hoover sign, collapsing weakness in both legs, entrainment of the right hand tremor, distractibility of gait, and convergence spasm with miosis. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (eyes closed and resisting opening, asynchronous limb jerking, side-to-side head movement, pelvic thrusting) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

interactions: Sertraline + cyclobenzaprine: cyclobenzaprine is structurally related to the tricyclic antidepressants, and serotonin syndrome has been reported with the combination. Monitor for agitation, tremor, myoclonus, hyperreflexia and hyperthermia; avoid the combination where possible.
Sertraline + ibuprofen: an SSRI with an NSAID raises the risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Use the lowest NSAID dose for the shortest time, or consider gastroprotection or paracetamol.
Lorazepam + cyclobenzaprine + levetiracetam: additive central nervous system depression (sedation, dizziness, impaired coordination).
general.proposed: Sertraline 100 mg once daily; Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg at bedtime as needed; Ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours as needed; Lorazepam 0.5 mg as needed for acute anxiety, max twice daily; Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily
general.summary: Clinically relevant: serotonergic toxicity with sertraline and cyclobenzaprine, gastrointestinal bleeding with sertraline and ibuprofen, additive sedation with lorazepam, cyclobenzaprine and levetiracetam, and sertraline-associated hyponatremia; levetiracetam has mood and behavioural adverse effects.
warnings: Levetiracetam: irritability, low mood and anxiety are recognised adverse effects. If it is discontinued, reduce the dose gradually.

Lorazepam (as needed, up to twice daily): sedation and dependence with regular use; it is not a rescue treatment for events not shown to be epileptic. After regular use, reduce gradually rather than stop abruptly.
Sertraline: hyponatremia from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion; monitor serum sodium.

activating_procedures.hyperventilation: Performed for 3 minutes. Normal symmetrical slowing as physiological response. No epileptiform discharges provoked. Patient reported feeling dizzy but no clinical event occurred.
activating_procedures.photic_stimulation: Performed at frequencies 1-30 Hz. Normal photic driving response. No photoparoxysmal response.

artifacts.description: Significant movement artifact during two captured clinical events, obscuring EEG but with readable underlying channels showing no epileptiform activity
Intermittent EMG artifact, does not obscure underlying cerebral activity during interictal periods

background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 10 Hz alpha rhythm, symmetric, well-modulated, reactive to eye opening
background.sleep_features: Normal sleep architecture with vertex waves, sleep spindles, and K-complexes. No epileptiform discharges in drowsiness or sleep.

findings.morphology: Patient alerted staff to an impending episode, then closed her eyes tightly; bilateral asynchronous limb jerking with side-to-side head movement and pelvic thrusting. EEG showed the normal awake background with superimposed movement artifact; no ictal pattern, no post-event slowing or attenuation.
findings.type: Clinical event 1 - bilateral asynchronous limb jerking

findings.morphology: Similar semiology, beginning shortly after a telephone call. No ictal EEG change; normal background before and after the event.
findings.type: Clinical event 2 - bilateral asynchronous limb jerking

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. Two habitual events were recorded (eyes closed, bilateral asynchronous limb jerking, side-to-side head movement and pelvic thrusting) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the events; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the events. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.
eeg.limitations: Movement artifact during clinical events partially obscured some channels, but sufficient channels remained interpretable to confirm absence of ictal EEG pattern.

labs.interpretation: Sodium 132 mEq/L (low) and chloride 93 mEq/L (low). Remaining results within reference ranges.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

additional_observations: No white matter lesions to suggest demyelinating disease
Normal basal ganglia and thalami bilaterally
Normal cervical spinal cord signal on sagittal sequences through the foramen magnum
mri.impression: Normal non-contrast MRI of the brain. No structural lesion, white matter lesion, infarction, hemorrhage or mass.

clinical_pearls: Hoover sign: hip extension is stronger during contralateral hip flexion against resistance than on direct testing.
Eyes closed and resisting opening during a convulsive-appearing event favours a functional seizure over an epileptic seizure, in which the eyes are usually open.
The diagnosis is framed positively: the nervous system is not damaged but is not functioning correctly, rather than 'we cannot find anything wrong'.
Functional seizures account for about 20-40% of admissions to epilepsy monitoring units for presumed refractory epilepsy.
Psychiatric comorbidity (depression, anxiety, PTSD) is present in most patients with functional seizures and is a treatment target, not a diagnostic criterion.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Mixed phenotype: functional seizures, functional leg weakness and functional tremor, with levetiracetam already started for presumed epilepsy. The examination gives five validated signs and an observed event, and the 72-hour video-EEG records two habitual events without ictal change; the agent must then review and taper the antiseizure drug, despite a grandmother with epilepsy and a strong stressor.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Pooja Iyer is a 42-year-old right-handed accountant who presents for inpatient evaluation after six weeks of progressive neurological symptoms that have left her unable to work. Her symptoms began approximately six weeks ago with an intermittent coarse tremor of the right hand that would come and go throughout the day, lasting minutes to hours at a time. She describes the tremor as most prominent when she is stressed or being observed, and she notes it sometimes stops when she is absorbed in an activity like reading to her children, only to return when she becomes aware of it again. Two weeks after the tremor onset, she began experiencing episodes of unresponsiveness accompanied by whole-body shaking. These episodes have occurred approximately eight times, most recently yesterday. Witnesses, including her estranged husband and her mother, describe episodes lasting one to three minutes during which she becomes unresponsive, her eyes close tightly, and she develops asynchronous bilateral jerking movements of her arms and legs. The movements are described as variable in speed and amplitude, sometimes waxing and waning. Her husband reports that during one episode, she appeared to be crying while shaking. After the episodes, she typically becomes tearful and states she cannot remember what happened, but she does not appear confused and is able to speak clearly within seconds of the episode ending. She has never injured herself during these events, never bitten her tongue, and has never been incontinent. Over the past three weeks, she has also developed progressive weakness in both legs, worse on the right than the left. She reports difficulty walking and has been using a cane provided by her primary care physician. She states the weakness is constant but seems worse on days when she is more stressed. She was initially seen at an outside emergency department four weeks ago after her second shaking episode, where a CT head was normal. She was started on levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily for presumed new-onset seizures. Despite the medication, her episodes have continued at the same frequency, which prompted referral to neurology. She was admitted two days ago for video-EEG monitoring. She reports significant life stressors including separation from her husband three months ago and an ongoing custody battle. She describes increased anxiety and difficulty sleeping since the separation. At age 19, during college, she had a similar period of shaking episodes that resolved spontaneously without treatment; she did not initially disclose this.

neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, the patient experienced a paroxysmal episode lasting approximately 90 seconds: she became unresponsive, eyes closed tightly with visible flutter, bilateral asynchronous jerking movements of all four extremities with variable amplitude and frequency, side-to-side head movements, and pelvic thrusting. No cyanosis. Her arms could be gently repositioned, and she resisted passive eye opening. Episode terminated gradually. Patient was tearful and reported no memory of the event. Throughout the event, she was able to avoid hitting the bedrail when her arm was passively dropped toward it.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing on the left is intact. Right heel-to-shin shows variable performance with inconsistent errors not following a cerebellar pattern. Rapid alternating movements normal bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive 4mm to 2mm. Fundoscopy normal, no papilledema. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact. Intermittent convergence spasm noted during testing with convergent eye deviation and miosis, resolving spontaneously. No sustained nystagmus. CN V: Sensation intact V1-V3 bilaterally, masseter strength symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation. CN VIII: Hearing intact to finger rub bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically, gag reflex intact. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline, no fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Walks with dramatic, lurching gait with excessive truncal sway but without falling. Demonstrates astasia-abasia pattern with marked swaying and flailing of arms but consistently catches herself. When asked to perform tandem gait, sways dramatically but does not fall. Gait improves significantly when distracted by cognitive tasks (serial subtraction). Romberg testing shows exaggerated sway with arms out, body swaying in multiple directions including forward and backward, inconsistent with true proprioceptive loss.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech fluent, normal rate and prosody. Affect mildly anxious but cooperative. Attention intact, able to spell WORLD backward. Memory 3/3 registration, 3/3 recall at 5 minutes. Language intact, no paraphasic errors. Fund of knowledge appropriate.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal in upper extremities. Variable resistance to passive movement in bilateral lower extremities, not velocity-dependent, inconsistent with spasticity or rigidity. Strength testing: Upper extremities 5/5 throughout bilaterally. Right lower extremity: Hip flexion 4/5 with give-way pattern (initial full effort followed by sudden collapse), knee extension 4/5 with give-way weakness, ankle dorsiflexion 3/5 with give-way pattern. Left lower extremity: Hip flexion 4-/5 with give-way pattern, knee extension 4/5 with give-way weakness, ankle dorsiflexion 4/5. Hoover sign positive bilaterally: involuntary hip extension noted when testing contralateral hip flexion, with significantly greater force generated involuntarily than during direct testing. No pronator drift in upper extremities. Intermittent coarse right hand tremor at rest and with posture, variable in frequency and amplitude; it takes on the rhythm of tapping with the left hand and pauses during ballistic left-hand movements.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus. Reflexes are normal and symmetric, inconsistent with the degree of reported weakness.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the entire right leg in a non-dermatomal distribution, with a sharp midline split extending to the trunk. Vibration sense reportedly absent in right leg but intact in left. However, tuning fork placed on the right side of the frontal bone of the skull reportedly not felt, which is physiologically inconsistent as bone conducts vibration bilaterally. Proprioception intact at bilateral great toes when formally tested with distraction.
